item.title: AIKO brings its fourth generation of back-contact solar to Australia
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Solar manufacturer AIKO has introduced its Gen 4 solar panels to Australia at All-Energy Australia in Melbourne. Built on ABC 4.0 INFINITE Ultra cell technology, the new range of all-back-contact solar panels delivers up to 20 W more per panel, without making panels bigger or heavier.
item.content:encoded:
For homes, Gen 4 brings 500 W performance to all-black panels in both dual-glass and mono-glass designs. For commercial and utility projects, the same performance upgrade extends across larger 60-, 66- and 72-cell formats.

Gen 4 reflects the growing maturity of back-contact technology. Over three generations, AIKO moved back contact from a premium niche into mainstream solar. With its fourth generation, the focus now shifts to maximising value for installers and customers on every roof.

What’s new in Gen 4?

In the new ABC 4.0 INFINITE Ultra cell, six process upgrades lift average production cell efficiency from 27.2% to 27.4%.

At the panel level, zero-gap cells, hidden rear connections (InvisiRibbon) and tighter string spacing cut non-generating area by about 20%, so 97% of the surface now produces power.

Every ABC INFINITE Ultra series format gains up to 20 W over the previous generation, at exactly the same size and weight. Against TOPCon panels of the same dimensions on the current market, that means up to 30 W more power per panel.

In the 54-cell size used on most Australian homes, where AIKO released the world’s first 500 W, 25% efficient white-backsheet panel under 2 m² in 2025, Gen 4 pushes further to 510 W and 25.5% efficiency.

AIKO Head of APAC Alex Hang said Australian households have had AIKO back-contact panels on their roofs for several years, and Australian installers have helped prove the technology in some of the toughest conditions in the world.

“The INFINITE Ultra series gives them more power from every roof, more ways to mount it, and the confidence that comes from technology built to last for decades,” Hang said.

“We never stop advancing, and we want Australia to be among the first to benefit.”

The INFINITE Ultra series also comes in a choice of larger formats to suit different projects. The 60-cell panel (1,954 × 1,134 mm) reaches 560 W, and the 72-cell panel (2,382 × 1,134 mm) reaches 700 W at 25.9% efficiency, the highest in the range.

Gen 4 also tackles back contact’s traditional weakness in rear-side generation, with the 66-cell bifacial panel now reaching up to 85% bifaciality and 670 W. This opens back contact to high-albedo sites, carports, ground-mounted systems and solar farms.

All-black 500 W: extreme power and aesthetics for Australia’s premium homes

For many owners of high-end homes, the look of solar has long been a reason to hold back. Visible gridlines, blue cell edges and uneven colour can clash with a carefully designed roof. And an all-black finish has historically come at the cost of performance, as older types of black panels typically run hotter and produce less power.

Gen 4 removes that trade-off, bringing 500 W and 25.0% efficiency to an all-black panel in the standard 1,762 × 1,134 mm size, with no visible gridlines and the same black colour between cells.

Homeowners are no longer forced to choose between a premium look and premium performance, and they can choose between two designs.

Z Series is the premium choice, with a uniform pure-black finish front and back. Its sharp look is paired with a stronger frame, enhanced reliability and dual-glass construction, which together support a 40-year product and power warranty, matching the life of a new roof. Z Series is already open for orders in Europe and is expected to be available in Australia in 2027.

Neostar Champion, part of the Gen 4 Neostar range, delivers the same 500 W all-black performance in a mono-glass design, backed by a 30-year product and power warranty.

Designed with installers in mind

As the industry races toward higher wattage, a common shortcut has been to simply make panels bigger or thinner. It produces an eye-catching number on the datasheet, but the cost falls on installers: heavier lifts, awkward non-standard sizes, and roof layouts and racking that must be reworked.

AIKO chose a different approach. The INFINITE Ultra series gains power from better technology rather than a bigger frame. Each panel keeps the same size and weight as the matching previous-generation panel, and the 54-cell panels stay under 2 m² and 25 kg.

Installers also get more ways to mount Gen 4, where approved in the installation manual: short-side or long-side clamping, with or without rails, and short-side or long-side insertion.

On the Z Series, an optimised structural design boosts the four-corner front-side mounting load from 1,600 Pa to 2,400 Pa. More watts per panel also means fewer panels, clamps and rails for the same system size, and AIKO’s local Australian team backs installers with training and technical support.

Value beyond wattage

With AIKO, customers don’t have to trade one benefit for another. Alongside higher output, the INFINITE Ultra series strengthens fire safety, reliability and long-term energy performance, addressing the operating conditions and asset-life considerations that matter to installers, EPCs and system owners. Features vary by model.

  • Fire safety. Anti-ignition features, active and passive fire protection and IEC Fire Class A, with hot-spot temperatures more than 35% lower than TOPCon under shading in TÜV Rheinland testing.
  • Reliability. Copper interconnection resists micro-cracking, with zero cracks recorded in TÜV NORD’s 230 kg treading test, while improved insulation and moisture resistance protect the panel edges.
  • Durability. Hail tested with 40 mm on specified mono-glass models.
  • Long-term performance. Low degradation, cell-level partial-shading optimisation and a low temperature coefficient help protect output under challenging Australian conditions, from partial shade to summer heat, over the life of the system.

What it means for Australian homes

Australia’s rooftops are being asked to do more than ever. Around 42% of homes already have solar, and more than 500,000 home batteries have been installed under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program since July 2025.

As households add batteries, EVs and heat pumps, the question is no longer whether to go solar, but how much a roof can deliver: more energy from limited space, with a finish that complements the home, and the confidence that it will last for decades.

Gen 4 is built around those priorities. With up to 30 W more per panel than TOPCon panels of the same size, homeowners can fit around 6% more solar capacity on the same roof. More generation means bigger savings, more solar to charge the home battery and fewer grid purchases in the evening. It also gives households the capacity to keep adding, from an EV to a heat pump or pool, on the path to a fully electrified home.

What it means for businesses

The expansion of the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme to systems up to 1 MW is a rare opportunity to bring more Australian businesses into commercial solar. By lowering upfront costs and improving project feasibility, it opens the benefits of renewable energy to a much broader segment of the economy.

To make the most of it, businesses need to get the most from every square metre of roof. High-efficiency panels like AIKO’s ABC INFINITE Ultra series do exactly that, unlocking higher system capacity and, with it, greater STC value.

For small or complex sites, that extra capacity can be the difference between a token installation and a system large enough to meaningfully support the business’s energy demand. And with multiple formats to suit different buildings, including a high power-to-weight ratio for weight-constrained roofs, more businesses can find the right fit.

Never stop advancing: delivering more value with every generation

Gen 4 reflects AIKO’s commitment to making high-performance back-contact solar accessible to every rooftop. Across its first three generations, AIKO focused on overcoming the technology and manufacturing barriers that had kept back contact in a premium niche.

By making mass production commercially viable and bringing the technology to more accessible price points, it helped move back contact into the mainstream, helping more homes and businesses enjoy better performance and greater value from solar.

Gen 4 builds on that foundation by addressing a wider range of customer needs and project constraints. Its significance goes beyond a higher number on the datasheet: it brings together output, installation flexibility, reliability, safety and design, rather than asking customers to choose one or two strengths.

The ambition is not simply to make back contact more accessible, but to make it deliver more: greater productivity from every roof, stronger project economics and lasting value over the life of the asset.

AIKO ANZ Head Thomas Bywater said the expanded scheme is a rare opportunity to bring more Australian businesses into solar, but it shouldn’t be wasted on poorly matched systems or short-term thinking.

“For business owners, installing solar is never abstract. Behind every commercial project is a business trying to manage costs, protect jobs and build a more resilient future, and it needs a system that delivers real returns, not just an incentive claim,” Bywater said.

“With the right technology and the right design for each site, the incentive will do more than reduce the cost of solar. It will help Australian businesses invest with confidence.”

item.title: Acid-free molten salt method recovers 94% of silver from solar cells
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Researchers in China have recovered 94.34% of the silver from crystalline silicon solar cells using an acid-free molten salt process that detaches the silver as metal, and have identified how to control silicon loss during treatment.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers in China have developed an acid-free method to recover silver wires from end-of-life aluminum back-surface-field solar cells using a molten mixture of sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide (NaOH-KOH).

The molten salt etches the cell’s silicon nitride (SiNx) passivation layer and weakens the bond between the silver and the SiNx, allowing the silver wires to detach and be recovered directly as metal, rather than being dissolved into silver ions and recovered later.

At 230 C for 150 seconds, the process recovered 94.34% of the silver and effectively removed the SiNx layer, the researchers said. Maximum silver recovery reached 97.11%.

Silicon substrate loss was limited to 2.62% at 230 C for 100 seconds. The researchers found that once the SiNx layer is removed, the exposed silicon is attacked by hydroxide ions in the molten salt, causing pitting and converting silicon into soluble sodium and potassium silicates.

The work builds on an earlier NaOH-KOH molten salt recycling approach reported in 2024. The researchers said existing molten salt methods avoid acids but do not effectively control silicon substrate loss, and that the new study clarifies the mechanisms behind both silver recovery and silicon loss.

Most silver recovery from end-of-life modules still relies on acid leaching with nitric acid and other strong acids, which converts silver into ions and generates nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions and acidic wastewater, according to the researchers. They noted that silver accounts for less than 0.03% of the weight of an end-of-life module but nearly half of its total value, and that the first generation of commercial PV modules is now reaching the end of its 25- to 30-year life.

The work was carried out at laboratory scale.

The findings appear in “Sustainable recovery of silver wires from crystalline silicon solar cells,” which was recently published in the Journal of Cleaner Production.

Researchers from Australia’s University of Newcastle, CSIRO Energy and PV Industries recently recovered an average of 93% of silver electrochemically from a simulated nitric acid leaching solution using stainless steel cathodes. Separately, researchers from the University of New South Wales, Gdansk University of Technology and the Polish Academy of Sciences found that silver can make up to 47% of a module’s recoverable value, though falling silver content in newer panels will lower future recycling revenue.

item.title: WA to legalise plug-in solar panels and batteries modelled on German standards
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Western Australia has announced it is taking steps to legalise plug-in solar panels and batteries, known colloquially as 'balcony solar', to benefit renters and apartment dwellers.
item.content:encoded:
In an Australian first, Western Australia is on the path to legalise plug-in solar panels and batteries based on German standards, which can plug in to a household wall outlet, offering clean energy for homes and apartments/units unable to benefit from rooftop solar installations and can also be moved when a resident changes address.

WA Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the benefits of cheap solar have been out of reach for anyone who doesn’t own their roof.

“That isn’t fair, and the Cook Labor Government is doing something about it,” Sanderson said.

“I’m proud that our State is leading the nation on this issue – millions of European households already use these systems every day, and WA families should be able to do the same.”

The WA department of Energy and Economic Diversification (DEED) and Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety’s Building and Energy Division (LGIRS) are consulting on the proposed legalisation pathway and a new technical standard.

The proposal would mean plug-in systems are classed as standard electrical appliances through a new Technical Bridging Standard (TBS), which proposes to enable plug-in systems with solar panel combinations up to a rated capacity of 2 kW (DC), and with inverters up to a rated capacity of 800 VA (AC).

The TBS does not propose to set an upper limit on plug-in battery storage capacity.

Balcony solar advocacy organisation Solar Citizens Chief Executive Officer Heidi Lee Douglas said it agrees it isn’t fair that the benefits of cheap solar are out of reach for anyone who doesn’t own their own roof.

“WA’s announcement starts a ‘race to the top’, and puts a rocket up the need for the federal government to announce a nationally coordinated approach for the release of this money-saving technology across Australia by July next year,” Douglas said.

“We support the Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen announcing a date for the legal safe sale of these money saving devices that are already legally and safely available in the United Kingdom, Germany and 10 states of America.“

“Plug-in solar and batteries are an anti-inflationary energy reform. They put downward pressure on household electricity bills, allow more Australians to use cheap solar power, and can reduce demand for expensive electricity during peak periods,” Douglas said.

According to the WA plug-in solar and batteries consultation website, DEED and LGIRS will continue to work with safety experts, other states and territories, and the Australian Government to support nationally consistent requirements for plug-in systems.

“For this reason, the final TBS is likely to have two separate parts, one each for product-specific requirements and another for installation requirements. This would make the TBS more consistent with AS/NZS technical documents,” the site says.

The department will also work on other changes that might be needed to support renter access to the systems once they are available.

item.title: CATL TENER+ BESS gets global debut while deep interest in TENER Sodium grows
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: CATL has conducted the global reveal of its 9 MWh TENER+ BESS at All Energy Melbourne 2026, and showcased the TENER Sodium-ion BESS, which the company said is attracting deep interest in Australia.
item.content:encoded:
China-headquartered energy storage manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) has conducted the global reveal of its 9 MWh TENER+ battery energy storage system (BESS) at All Energy Australia 2026, where it also showcased the TENER Sodium BESS, indicating there is deep interest to progress the technology in Australia, for both on and off-grid projects.

CATL Australia and New Zealand General Manager Zane Zhou told pv magazine sodium is an important part of CATL’s strategy and there is significant interest for its sodium batteries in Australia.

“Not just in the National Electricity Market (NEM) but also for off-grid applications,” Zhou confirmed.

“Australia is a strategic market for CATL and one of the great renewable energy markets where we have received very deep interest in sodium batteries.”

Zhou said having both lithium-ion and sodium-ion platforms however gives CATL and its customers more options.

TENER+ BESS

The TENER+ is a 9 MWh ultra-high capacity energy storage system that reduces the number of containers needed by 40% and the project footprint by 35%, making it ideal for projects that are facing land constraints.

CATL said the TENER+ intelligent thermal management system supports a higher round-trip efficiency and lower auxiliary power consumption. Multiple TENER+ batteries can be simultaneously commissioned with a single click to streamline project deployment.

Designed for a 25-year lifespan, TENER+ also combines liquid cooling with protection suited to humid and coastal environments. It operates below 65 dBA without heat-island effects, making it suitable for deployment near residential communities. Its thermal management strategies maintain cells at optimal operating temperatures to support its performance over the battery’s lifespan.

TENER Sodium

TENER Sodium is one of the world’s first mass-produced, field-validated sodium-ion battery energy storage systems delivering more than 30 MWh through its modular cabinet architecture and lowers total EPC costs by more than 10% when compared to lithium iron phosphate battery (LFP) containerised energy storage solutions. 

Built for Australia’s heat, TENER Sodium operates in temperatures of up to 55°C and delivers more than 10,000 cycles at 45°C. It delivers 95% round-trip efficiency with an operating lifespan of more than 20 years. 

“Developers need confidence that their batteries can handle the expected cycling to trade in the National Electricity Market and to perform throughout the lifespan of batteries installed in a utility-scale project,” Zhou said.

“That is what TENER+ and TENER Sodium are designed to deliver. We’re offering both sodium-ion and lithium-ion technologies to give asset owners and developers the flexibility to choose the right technology for their success.”

Sodium is also more abundant and geographically widespread than lithium and delivers an additional pathway for battery supply chains.

Local industry partnerships

Recognising an increasing need in Australia for energy storage systems with grid-forming capability as coal-fired power stations retire, along with addressing skills, grid connections and integration risks for large-scale battery projects, CATL also signed at All Energy, three Memorandum of Understandings (MoUs) respectively with the Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and the University of New South Wales (UNSW) Sydney.

“CATL is working with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group, ESVL and UNSW Sydney to give our Australian customers greater confidence in how our technology is integrated, validated and supported throughout a project’s life. Together, we’re building the local expertise needed to deliver reliable battery projects in the long-term,” Zhou said.

CATL’s DC battery products and Hitachi Energy’s power conversion systems will form the basis of a proposed integrated offering in Australia and the Asia Pacific region, with the partnership aiming to improve compatibility, standardise project delivery and to reduce integration risk.

A collaboration with EPEC Group and the Xiamen Empirical Energy Storage Research Institute (ESVL) will combine CATL’s energy storage technology with EPEC’s grid integration and engineering delivery expertise, and ESVL’s full-scale system validation.

The parties aim to strengthen technical validation and accelerate the delivery of reliable, bankable and grid-compliant energy storage projects in Australia.

A strategic partnership with UNSW Sydney includes jointly developing a Centre for Integrated Renewable Energy Training and Innovation (CIRETI) in Western Sydney, NSW, to advance the skills and capabilities needed for Australia’s clean energy transition.

Birdwood Energy

The MoUs build on CATL’s work with Australian customers, including Melbourne-based investor Birdwood Energy, which has selected CATL as the technology partner for the Barandudua Electrical Energy Reserve, a 400 MW /1,860 MWh battery near Wodonga in Victoria.

Birdwood Australia Managing Director Alex Marriott-Smith said Baranduda is a key project for Birdwood’s Australian business and its investors.

“Identifying the right technology and delivery partners for the project was therefore critical during the procurement phase. Following a rigorous process that reviewed cost, product suitability and delivery requirements, CATL was selected to provide the project’s battery units.,” Marriott-Smith said.”

Zhou added that CATL’s commitment to Australia goes beyond supplying energy storage systems.

“We’re investing in people, partnerships and capability, from training the next generation of renewable energy professionals to working with our customers and partners to connect and deliver the critical projects Australia’s grid needs,” Zhou said.

CATL has led global energy storage battery shipments for five consecutive years, with a 30.4% market share in 2025, according to SNE Research. It has been on BloombergNEF’s Tier 1 energy storage list every quarter since Q1 2024. CATL has more than 3,000 energy storage projects worldwide and an installed capacity of over 17GWh of projects in Australia.

item.title: Better bushfire smoke forecasting could improve solar farm output
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Researchers from the University of New South Wales have found that smoke from major bushfires can reduce solar electricity generation by 70% at solar farms as far as 150 kilometres away.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers from the University of New South Wales (UNSW) Sydney have found that smoke from major bushfires can reduce solar electricity generation by 70%, and up to 30% at solar farms as far as 150 kilometres away.

The researchers recommend better forecasting of smoke movements, more frequent panel inspections and cleaning, and changes to how solar panels operate to help operators prepare for bushfire events and protect equipment.

Using historical weather and satellite data, the researchers modelled how smoke and airborne particles affected solar electricity generation and panel temperatures across south-eastern Australia by examining the effects of the 2019-2020 Black Summer fires and Victoria’s 2009 Black Saturday fires.

Conducted by the UNSW School of Photovoltaic and Renewable Energy Engineering (SPREE), researchers estimate during the Black Summer bushfires electricity generation fell by as much as 70% at locations within about 50 kilometres of fire hotspots during several consecutive days.

In regions more than 150 kilometres from hotspots, the study estimated there were still losses of up to 30%.

“Even at a radius of 150 kilometres away from the hotspots, there was around 30% reduction on, or just after, the bushfire days, because a lot of the wind had transported the smoke inland across New South Wales,” SPREE Postdoctoral Researcher Dr Shukla Poddar said.

In the 2009 Black Saturday bushfires, the study estimated lower reductions of generated power of around 18% near fire hotspots and up to 10% in more distant regions.

The figures are modelled estimates rather than measurements from individual solar farms and the researchers were unable to separate smoke-related losses from other factors, such as electricity generation being deliberately curtailed.

Poddar said the research highlights the need to look beyond solar farms immediately surrounding a fire and consider where smoke is likely to travel.

“We should start looking into things like trajectory modelling of the smoke and how long and far those smoke particles can be transported,” Poddar said.

“Extreme bushfires are becoming more frequent and intense in several regions, including Australia, California and southern Europe. Their impacts are not confined to the areas where fires burn: smoke from California’s 2020 wildfires reached Europe, while smoke from Spain’s 2025 fires travelled as far as the UK and northwestern Europe.”

Poddar added that although this particular study is based on two extreme bushfires in Australia, the same method and analysis can be done for other parts of the world.

A key recommendation from the study is to combine bushfire information, wind patterns and smoke-trajectory modelling to help predict which solar farms are likely to be affected, similar to weather forecast systems already in use for monitoring temperatures and wind.

The research suggests warnings could allow operators to plan inspections, schedule cleaning or adjust the position of panels before smoke arrives.

“If operators got an alert that their solar farm might be impacted, they could potentially adapt some mitigation strategies, such as adjusting the panel angle where appropriate or being aware that additional cleaning may be required,” Poddar said.

Panel maintenance, particularly during bushfire periods, was also advised to avoid reduced sunlight on panel surfaces or the build up of localised hot spots due to uneven soot accumulation. Poddar recommends more frequent cleaning when smoke is likely to affect a solar farm, alongside regular thermal inspections to identify unusually hot panels or electrical components.

The research finds that better remote monitoring and electrical fault detection would also allow operators to identify temperature anomalies and quickly isolate affected parts of a system, along with managing grass and shrubs beneath panels, maintaining firebreaks and preparing bushfire management plans can help reduce the risk of fires starting or spreading within solar farms.

These and further findings in the ‘Understanding non-localised impacts of bushfires on photovoltaic performance, reliability, and management strategies’ paper have been published in the Solar Energy journal.

item.title: Fortescue signs first green grid 20-year power deal with Pilbara lithium miner
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Perth-headquartered mining giant Fortescue has pushed forward on its intent to supply industry in the Pilbara with renewable energy by signing a 20-year power purchase agreement with an Australian lithium mining company.
item.content:encoded:
Perth-headquartered mining giant Fortescue has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Australian lithium mining company PLS Group, marking the first external deal associated with Fortescue’s Green Grid, a renewable energy network built to power its own and other industry operations in the Pilbara, Western Australia.

By 2028, Fortescue’s Green Grid is anticipated to include 1.5 GW of solar generation, 900 MW wind generation, 4-5 GWh of battery storage and what the company describes as the “world’s largest” inverter-based grid.

Under the 20-year agreement, Fortescue has committed to supply a minimum 325 GWh of power annually to PLS’ Pilgangoora Operation, or the equivalent of the annual electricity use of approximately 45,000 homes.

With supply expected to commence in 2029, the PPA will help power the lithium miner’s recently approved $1.9 billion (USD 1.3 billion) expansion.

PLS will fund an approximatley 25-kilometre, 220 kV transmission line to connect the Pilgangoora Operation to Fortescue’s Green Grid. PLS will own 20 kilometres of the line, with Fortescue owning the rest.

Fortescue has already built 550 kilometres of a planned 660-kilometre transmission line network across the Pilbara.

Fortescue Metals Chief Executive Officer Dino Otranto said the Green Grid was initially started to power the company’s mining, rail and port operations, but the demand for cheap, green, reliable power across the Pilbara was an opportunity to supply other customers too.

“Cost. Climate. Control. That’s the case for the Green Grid. We used 680 million litres of diesel last year, and every 10-cent rise in diesel prices adds almost $99.3 million to our annual costs,” Otranto said.

“Replacing diesel with renewable power improves our competitiveness, cuts emissions, reduces our exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices and gives us greater control over when and where we use energy.”

Otranto said the agreement is an important first step and cements Fortescue’s role as an energy supplier.

“PLS is our first customer, with a strong pipeline of others across the Pilbara looking to our Green Grid for greater choice and flexibility in how they source their power,” Otranto said.

PLS Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Dale Henderson added the PPA will deliver lower-cost, lower-emissions power to the company’s approximatley 20-year long Pilgangoora operation.

“[It is] further strengthening our competitiveness in the global lithium industry,” Henderson said.

item.title: Atmoce targets commercial and industrial sector with its flexible AC stackable storage
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Atmoce has introduced its AC stackable extra-low voltage storage solution in Australia and follows the September start of the peak demand reduction battery incentive scheme for businesses in NSW.
item.content:encoded:
Germany-headquartered energy technology company Atmoce is launching its AC stackable extra-low voltage storage solution in Australia and follows the September 2026 start of the Peak Demand Reduction Scheme (PDRS) for commercial and industrial (C&I) businesses in New South Wales (NSW).

Introducing the M-ELV BattBank in Australia at All Energy Australia 2026, the new solution comprises a modular AC architecture operating below 60 V DC, with each BattBank cluster accommodating up to seven battery packs, delivering up to 112 kWh.

Capacity can be expanded in 16 kWh increments to suit individual site requirements.

Independent module operation helps support system continuity if a battery module fails, while 0.25C–0.5C adjustable power enables peak shaving and energy shifting.

Atmoce said the solution’s modular, scalable architecture is well suited to the expanded NSW PDRS, including battery energy storage system (BESS)5 installations above 200 kWh and up to 30 MWh.

Since 1 September 2026, eligible C&I installations in NSW can receive approximately 20–40% discounts through the PDRS scheme, depending on the installation.

15-year M-ELV Battery Warranty for Australia

Atmoce has also extended the warranty for its residential M-ELV Battery (MS-7K-U) to 15 years, which provides coverage for 15 years or 29.2 MWh of energy throughput, with a minimum 60% state of health retained, whichever comes first.

The M-ELV battery uses an extra-low voltage AC architecture operating below 30 Vdc, designed to reduce risks associated with high-voltage DC while supporting flexible residential energy system integration.

The warranty is Australia-wide and extends to eligible MS-7K-U units already shipped or being installed.

item.title: SMA grid-forming DC-hybrid solution unveiled at All Energy Australia
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: SMA Australia has unveiled a new grid-forming solar and battery solution at All Energy Australia, which tackles the key developer challenges of securing grid connections and attracting investment.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-based SMA Australia, a subsidiary of German solar and battery inverter manufacturer SMA Solar Technology AG, has unveiled a new grid-forming solution at All Energy in Melbourne, which tackles the challenges of securing grid connections and attracting investment.

The solution enables renewable generation to actively support electricity system stability through services including synthetic inertia, fast frequency response and voltage support.

Its DC-coupled architecture can capture solar energy otherwise lost through inverter clipping and storing it for dispatch during periods of higher electricity demand or more favourable market conditions.

It combines power conversion technology, intelligent plant controls and engineering support, helping reduce system integration complexity and the challenge of coordinating equipment and control systems from multiple suppliers.

It also incorporates advanced silicon carbide semiconductor technology, enabling DC-side conversion efficiencies of up to 99.%.

SMA Australia Managing Director John Alexander, who will address All Energy on Wednesday 28 October in a presentation titled ‘From megawatts to megabankable: How grid stability is reshaping renewable energy finance’, said the next phase of Australia’s energy transition won’t be measured by how many projects are announced but by how many actually connect to the grid, perform reliably and deliver a return.

“Grid stability is no longer just an engineering issue. It goes directly to investment confidence and long-term project value,” Alexander said.

“Developers and investors need confidence that their assets can perform reliably today and adapt to the needs of tomorrow’s electricity system. That means designing for Australia’s unique grid conditions, managing risk from the outset and preparing for evolving grid requirements and future market opportunities.”

Alexander said Australia has some of the most demanding grid connection requirements in the world and developers need more than technology that performs well in isolation.

“They need integrated solutions designed for Australian conditions, backed by local engineering expertise and long-term support,” Alexander said.

Medium voltage power station

Also on display at All Energy, SMA will showcase its 40-foot Medium Voltage Power Station (MVPS) 6400–10000 range.

Its integrated architecture, featuring redundant inverter technology, is designed to improve plant availability and support reliable operation of large-scale renewable energy projects.

Other power infrastructure solutions for artificial intelligence (AI) and hyperscale data centres displayed at the SMA Australia exhibit include GridAssist, GridLink AC and the planned GridLink DC architecture.

item.title: Trinasolar targets rooftops with ‘Australian-exclusive’ full-black module
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Trinasolar has announced an Australian-exclusive all-black version of its Vertex S+ G3 dual-glass TOPCon modules for residential and commercial applications. The new products deliver up to 510 W of power output with 24.4% efficiency.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese PV module manufacturer Trinasolar will unveil a full-black dual-glass TOPCon solar module for residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) applications at the All Energy Australia conference starting in Melbourne on Wednesday.

Edison Zhou, Trina’s head of operations in Australia, New Zealand and Pacific Islands, said the “Australian-exclusive” Vertex S+ G3 Full Black solar module marks the return of the company’s all-black offering, combining its distinctive design with next-generation TOPCon 3.0 technology.

“Black is back with more power, greater efficiency and next-generation solar technology,” he said. “The Vertex S+ G3 combines the premium all-black design customers want with the performance and reliability they expect from Trinasolar.”

The Vertex S+ G3 is built on Trinasolar’s n-type i-TOPCon Ultra technology, and features “zero-gap” stacked welding and “zero-string bar” technologies.

Trinasolar is offering five variants, with power output ranging from 490 W to 510 W and power conversion efficiencies between 23.5% and 24.4%. Open-circuit voltage ranges from 39.4 V to 40.0 V, while short-circuit current is between 15.91 A and 15.97 A.

The panels feature 1.6 mm glass front and back in a black anodised aluminium frame. They measure 1,842 mm x 1,134 mm x 30 mm and weigh 21.95 kg.

They can be deployed in systems with a maximum voltage of 1,500 V and feature IP68-rated junction boxes. The temperature coefficient is -0.26% per C, with an operating temperature range of -40 C to 70 C.

The modules are backed by a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year performance warranty. First-year degradation is specified at less than 1.0%, with 30-year end-of-life output guaranteed at no less than 88.5% of nominal power.

Trinasolar said the new panels are compatible with mainstream inverters and diverse mounting systems and have been manufactured in response to “strong demand from Australian homeowners, businesses and installers for high-performance solar that doesn’t compromise on appearance.”

The Vertex S+ G3 is part of a broader product portfolio that Trinasolar will unveil at All Energy.

The company will also use the event to launch its C&I Integrated Engineering & Solutions product, that will combine project-specific engineering, system optimisation and selective components sourcing, including solar modules, mounting and tracking systems, and battery energy storage solutions (BESS).

Trinasolar said the expansion of the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) on 1 October 2026 to qualifying solar installations above 100 kW and up to 1 MW creates new opportunities for C&I solar.

“As C&I projects increasingly integrate solar, battery storage and energy management technologies, Trina Solutions provides tailored support through close consultation with a dedicated team, leveraging global engineering experience to address immediate priorities and anticipate future needs,” the company said, adding  that “businesses and developers can benefit from integrated energy solutions, while EPCs and system integrators can leverage Trinasolar’s technologies and expertise to complement their existing capabilities for end-to-end project execution.”

Trinasolar also said it would use the All Energy event to showcase its wider solar and energy storage portfolio, including the 6.25 MWh Elementa 3 battery, which brings together DC technology with AC-side integration capabilities.

item.title: Western Australia targets 75% renewables share for main grid
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Western Australia has committed to a renewable energy target of 75% by 2030-2031 for its main electricity grid as it prepares for the retirement of state-owned coal-fired power stations by the end of this decade.
item.content:encoded:
The Western Australia (WA) government aims to achieve 75% renewable electricity on the South West Interconnected System (SWIS) by 2030-2031, supported by large-scale solar, wind, and battery energy storage projects.

The target doubles the previous goal of 40% and comes as the state prepares to exit coal-fired power by 2030.

The state government said the renewable energy target (RET) is complemented by a Made in WA Energy Affordability Investment Program that will provide low-interest loans of up to $15 million (USD 10.5 million) to help manufacturers install solar and battery systems and upgrade equipment to take advantage of cheaper energy. 

WA Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the new 75% target is a “statement of intent” that is designed to encourage private sector investment.

“We know that renewables, backed by storage and gas, is the cheapest and most reliable energy mix for Western Australia,” she said. “That’s why we’re powering ahead with our support for the energy opportunities of the future and encouraging businesses to invest in WA.”

The government’s commitment has been welcomed by climate advocacy collaborative Solutions for Climate WA and its alliance of business, industry, investors, unions, and advocacy bodies.

Solutions for Climate WA Director Jessica Panegyres said the new target is a key step forward for the state’s energy future.

“[This] makes it clear that the future of our electricity system is renewables,” she said. “A renewable energy target sends an important signal to the businesses, investors, workers and communities who will deliver WA’s next generation of energy infrastructure.”

WA has some of the best renewable energy resources in the world and a strong industrial base and Panegyres said setting a target provides the certainty required to turn that potential into investment on the ground.

Panegyres said the next task is making sure WA has a credible pathway to achieve its goal.

“That means continuing to accelerate investment in renewable energy generation, storage and the transmission infrastructure needed to connect it, while ensuring communities and regional areas share in the benefits,” she said.

Smart Energy Council (SEC) State Manager John Welch said WA’s new renewable energy target will advance the rate of growth for the state’s renewable energy industry

“Our members across solar, wind and battery storage are ready to build in WA, and a target gives them a clear goal to build towards,” he said, adding that transmission will be critical to achieving the target.

“The priority now is to keep the grid build moving and lock in dates for its next stages,” he said.
